subject: physiology
title: Splanchnic Circulation, Circulatory Shock, and Exercise

steps.tx: The abdominal viscera receive twenty-five percent of resting cardiac output (approximately one point four litres per minute) via the celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries, forming the **splanchnic circulation**. Venous drainage from the stomach, intestines, pancreas, and spleen converges into the portal vein, delivering nutrients directly to the liver before entering systemic circulation.
steps.say: The splanchnic circulation receives a quarter of resting cardiac output, draining through the portal vein into the liver before reaching the heart.

vis.alt: Splanchnic circulation and portal venous hemodynamics.
vis.caption: Splanchnic vascular bed and portal venous capacitance reservoirs. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Splanchnic blood flow surges dramatically following food ingestion, a phenomenon termed **postprandial hyperaemia**. Blood flow doubles within thirty minutes of a meal and remains elevated for hours, driven by local metabolic metabolites, cholecystokinin, secretin, neurotensin, and kinins, diverting blood from skeletal muscle and skin into digestive mucosa.
steps.say: Following food intake, postprandial hyperaemia doubles splanchnic blood flow, driven by digestive hormones and local metabolites to absorb nutrients.

nodes.label: Nutrient Ingestion and Chyme Entry into Duodenum
Local Secretion of Cholecystokinin, Secretin, Gastrin, and VIP
Direct Vasodilation of Mesenteric Mucosal Arterioles
Splanchnic Perfusion Surges up to Two-Fold for Active Absorption

steps.tx: Acute severe intravascular volume loss produces **haemorrhagic shock**, characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular lactic acidosis. Loss of twenty percent of blood volume reduces mean systemic filling pressure and preload. Baroreceptor unloading unleashes a maximal sympathetic discharge, inducing intense splanchnic, renal, and cutaneous vasoconstriction to preserve blood flow to the brain and heart.
steps.say: Haemorrhagic shock reduces venous return and cardiac output, unleashing massive sympathetic vasoconstriction to preserve perfusion to the brain and heart.

vis.alt: Hemodynamic pathophysiology of haemorrhagic shock and compensation.
vis.caption: Compensatory neuroendocrine and vascular responses during haemorrhagic shock. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Compensatory physiological mechanisms operate in three temporal phases. Rapid neural compensation via baroreceptors and chemoreceptors increases heart rate and peripheral resistance within seconds. Intermediate humoral compensation mobilises renin, angiotensin II, vasopressin, and adrenaline, while delayed **fluid shift** reclaims interstitial fluid into capillaries via autotransfusion.
steps.say: Shock compensation progresses from immediate baroreflex vasoconstriction to hormonal activation, followed by autotransfusion of interstitial fluid into capillaries.

rows: Sustained vasoconstriction and renal sodium retention
Starling shift (fall in Pc causes autotransfusion)
Up to 1 litre of interstitial fluid reabsorbed into plasma
Complete restoration of red cell mass and plasma volume

steps.tx: During vigorous dynamic physical exercise, the cardiovascular system undergoes dramatic hemodynamic redistribution. Cardiac output increases up to five-fold (from five to twenty-five litres per minute) through concurrent elevations in heart rate and stroke volume. Blood flow to **active skeletal muscle** surges twenty-fold, driven by local metabolic vasodilation that overrides systemic sympathetic vasoconstriction.
steps.say: During exercise, cardiac output surges up to five-fold, diverting eighty-five percent of blood flow to active skeletal muscle through metabolic vasodilation.

left.title: Resting Hemodynamics
points: Skeletal muscle receives 20% of cardiac output (1.0 L/min)

right.title: Heavy Exercise Hemodynamics
points: Cardiac output surges up to 25 litres per minute
Skeletal muscle receives 85% of output (20 to 22 L/min)
Renal blood flow restricted to 3% (0.75 L/min)

steps.tx: Exercise alters arterial pressures in a characteristic divergent pattern. Intense muscular vasodilation reduces total systemic vascular resistance. However, massive stroke volume ejection widens pulse pressure, elevating **systolic blood pressure** up to two hundred millimetres of mercury while diastolic pressure remains unchanged or falls slightly due to low peripheral resistance.
steps.say: During exercise, systolic pressure rises with large stroke volumes while diastolic pressure remains flat or falls due to muscular vasodilation.

nodes.label: Dynamic Muscle Exercise Accelerates Heart Rate and Stroke Volume
Large Stroke Volume Ejection Elevates Systolic BP (up to 200 mmHg)
Profound Metabolic Vasodilation in Skeletal Muscle Reduces Total SVR
Diastolic Blood Pressure Remains Constant or Decreases Slightly

steps.tx: Upon assuming an upright standing posture, gravity pools five hundred millilitres of blood into compliant lower extremity veins. This abrupt reduction in central venous volume triggers transient **postural hypotension**. Normal baroreceptor reflexes immediately induce reflex tachycardia and splanchnic vasoconstriction to restore pressure within seconds; reflex failure produces orthostatic syncope.
steps.say: Standing pools 500 mL of blood in leg veins, transiently dropping venous return. Baroreceptors fire reflex vasoconstriction to prevent orthostatic syncope.

left.title: Normal Orthostatic Response
points: Venous pooling in lower limbs decreases preload
Heart rate rises by 10 to 20 beats per minute
Diastolic pressure rises slightly; systolic drops < 10 mmHg

right.title: Orthostatic Hypotension (Autonomic Failure)
points: Defective baroreceptor reflex or severe hypovolaemia
Systolic drop > 20 mmHg or diastolic drop > 10 mmHg
Failure of compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction
Cerebral hypoperfusion produces lightheadedness and syncope

steps.tx: The commonest cause of fainting in healthy individuals is **vasovagal syncope**, also known as neurocardiogenic syncope. Triggered by emotional distress, prolonged standing, or heat, unexpected paradoxical ventricular mechanoreceptor activation unleashes a surge of vagal outflow combined with sudden withdrawal of sympathetic tone, causing severe bradycardia, profound vasodilation, and cerebral hypoperfusion.
steps.say: Vasovagal syncope occurs when emotional triggers elicit paradoxical vagal excitation and sympathetic withdrawal, causing bradycardia, vasodilation, and fainting.

rows: Emotional stress, fear, prolonged warm standing
Blunted sympathetic response to postural pooling
Primary mechanical or electrical pump arrest
Nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, yawn, tunnel vision
Sudden collapse with zero warning aura
